```{r population}
# A population of users, each with an engagement score nobody records.
make_users <- function(n) data.frame(engagement = rnorm(n))

# The chance a user converts. More engaged users convert more. A treated user's
# chance goes up by `lift`, in absolute terms: lift = 0.005 is half a
# percentage point.
p_convert <- function(engagement, treated = 0, lift = 0)
  plogis(-3 + 0.8 * engagement) + lift * treated

# Whether each user converts, given their chances.
convert <- function(p) rbinom(length(p), 1, p)
```

# Part 1 · Who chose the treatment (14 points)
```{r}
set.seed(6101)
u <- make_users(20000)
u$converted <- convert(p_convert(u$engagement)) # did they convert? yes/no
u$opted_in  <- rbinom(nrow(u), 1, plogis(-1 + 1.5 * u$engagement))
u$assigned  <- sample(rep(0:1, each = nrow(u) / 2))
```


## (1a) Opted in against not
```{r}

k_opted <- sum(u$converted[u$opted_in == 1])
k_notopt <- sum(u$converted[u$opted_in == 0])

n_opted <- sum(u$opted_in == 1)
n_notopt <- sum(u$opted_in == 0)

rate_opted <- k_opted / n_opted 
rate_notopt <- k_notopt / n_notopt

diff_rate <- abs(rate_opted - rate_notopt)

mod_opted <- prop.test(c(k_opted, k_notopt), c(n_opted, n_notopt), correct = FALSE)


```

Conversion rate of those who opted in: `r round(rate_opted, 3)`

Conversion rate of those who did not opt in: `r round(rate_notopt, 3)`

Difference in conversion rates: `r round(diff_rate, 3)`

P-value: `r format.pval(mod_opted$p.value, digits = 2, eps = 0.001)`


## (1b) Assigned at random
```{r}

k_assign <- sum(u$converted[u$assigned == 1])
k_notassign <- sum(u$converted[u$assigned == 0])

n_assign <- sum(u$assigned == 1)
n_notassign <- sum(u$assigned == 0)

rate_assign <- k_assign / n_assign
rate_notassign <- k_notassign / n_notassign

diff_rate_assign <- abs(rate_assign - rate_notassign)

mod_assign <- prop.test(c(k_assign, k_notassign), c(n_assign, n_notassign), correct = FALSE)

```

Conversion rate of assigned: `r round(rate_assign, 3)`

Conversion rate of not assigned: `r round(rate_notassign, 3)`

Difference in conversion rates: `r round(diff_rate_assign, 3)`

P-value: `r format.pval(mod_assign$p.value, digits = 2, eps = 0.001)`


## (1c) What the opt-in comparison measured
```{r}
mean(u$engagement[u$opted_in == 1])    # opted in
mean(u$engagement[u$opted_in == 0])    # did not opt in
mean(u$engagement[u$assigned == 1])    # assigned
mean(u$engagement[u$assigned == 0])    # not assigned
```

In part A, the opted in conversion is based on those who are inherently more engaged and more likely to convert, it is self-selection bias. In part B, users are randomized, this more-engaged behavior is more equally distributed, so a group "opted in" is not based on self-selection but created from randomization. Since engagement is not record, this would be a case of omitted variable bias, neither part A or B can correct for this since it wasn't actually measured.

# Part 2 · The sample size, before any data (14 points)

## (2a) The baseline, and the users per arm
```{r}
p0 <- mean(p_convert(u$engagement)) #baseline conversion rate
p0

pw_05 <- power.prop.test(p1 = p0, p2 = p0 + 0.005, power = 0.80, sig.level = 0.05) # 0.5 point increase
pw_10 <- power.prop.test(p1 = p0, p2 = p0 + 0.010, power = 0.80, sig.level = 0.05) # 1.0 point increase

ceiling(pw_05$n)   # users per arm, 0.5 pp
ceiling(pw_10$n)   # users per arm, 1.0 pp

```

The needed sample size to detect a 0.5 percentage point increase from a
baseline of `r round(p0, 3)` is n = `r format(ceiling(pw_05$n), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)`
per arm. For a 1.0 percentage point increase, n = `r format(ceiling(pw_10$n), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)`
per arm is needed.


## (2b) How many weeks
```{r}

weeks_05 <- 2 * ceiling(pw_05$n) / 4000
weeks_10 <- 2 * ceiling(pw_10$n) / 4000

weeks_05
ceiling(weeks_05)

weeks_10
ceiling(weeks_10)

```

For a 0.5 point increase, `r ceiling(weeks_05)` weeks are required to reach the requisite sample size. For a 1.0 point increase, `r ceiling(weeks_10)` weeks are needed.

## (2c) For the product manager
To achieve a 0.5 point increase, it requires `r ceiling(weeks_05)` weeks, which exceeds the month timeline. If we extend the timeline then we can detect the 0.5 point increase assuming we achieve the required sample size of `r format(ceiling(pw_05$n), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)` per arm. If we want to stick to the month timeline, we need to give up being able to detect the 0.5 point increase, but should be able to detect a 1.0 point increase. So we must weight time constraints with reaching a detectable effect size.

# Part 3 · Looking every day (20 points)

## (3a) One look against ten
```{r}

set.seed(6101)
looks <- seq(1000, 10000, by = 1000)

sims <- replicate(2000, {
  a <- convert(p_convert(rnorm(10000)))   
  b <- convert(p_convert(rnorm(10000)))   
  c(cumsum(a)[looks], cumsum(b)[looks])   
})


ka <- sims[1:10, ]    # cumulative conversions, arm a: rows = looks, cols = experiments
kb <- sims[11:20, ]   # cumulative conversions, arm b

p_mat <- sapply(1:2000, function(j)
  sapply(1:10, function(i)
    prop.test(c(ka[i, j], kb[i, j]), c(looks[i], looks[i]), correct = FALSE)$p.value))
# 10 x 2000

fp_end  <- mean(p_mat[10, ] < 0.05)
fp_peek <- mean(apply(p_mat < 0.05, 2, any))
fp_end
fp_peek


```

Running the experiment through to the end gives the desired false positive rate of about 5%, specifically, `r fp_end`. Whereas terminating early give a false positive rate of `r fp_peek`.


## (3b) When the false alarms happen, and a stricter threshold
```{r}

sig <- p_mat < 0.05               
stopped <- apply(sig, 2, any)            # stopped experiments
first_look <- apply(sig, 2, function(x) which(x)[1])   # NA if never significant

mean(first_look[stopped] <= 3)           # share of stopped at looks 1-3

# stricter threshold
fp_005 <- mean(apply(p_mat < 0.005, 2, any))   # stop at first look with p < 0.005
fp_005

```

Among the experiments stopped by the analyst, `r round(mean(first_look[stopped] <= 3), 3) ` of them were stopped within the first three times the analyst looked. Using a stricter threshold for experiments that were stopped, brings the false positive rate down to `r fp_005`.


## (3c) Why, and the stopping rule
Stopping the experiment early results in the most noise in the data, and a larger false positive rate (`r fp_peek`) from too small of a sample size. Even though having a stricter threshold brought the rate down (`r fp_005`), it's becomes increasingly harder for subsquent looks to actually pass which limits the power to detect a true positive. To maintain power at 80%, a larger sample size is needed for the stricter threshold.


# Part 4 · Count before you compare (14 points)
```{r}
set.seed(6101)
v <- make_users(40000)
v$arm <- sample(rep(0:1, each = nrow(v) / 2))
v$converted <- convert(p_convert(v$engagement))
lost <- v$arm == 1 & v$engagement < -0.5 & runif(nrow(v)) < 0.30
logged <- v[!lost, ]
```


## (4a) The split, then the outcome
```{r}

n_logged <- table(logged$arm)          # logged users per arm (0 = control, 1 = treatment)
n_logged
chisq.test(n_logged, p = c(0.5, 0.5))  # sample ratio check against 50/50

k1 <- sum(logged$converted[logged$arm == 1])
n1 <- sum(logged$arm == 1)
k0 <- sum(logged$converted[logged$arm == 0])
n0 <- sum(logged$arm == 0)

k1 / n1                                # treatment rate
k0 / n0                                # control rate
diff_conv_rate <- k1 / n1 - k0 / n0                      # difference, treatment minus control (keep the sign)
mod_split <- prop.test(c(k1, k0), c(n1, n0), correct = FALSE)

```

n arm1 = `r n0`

n arm2 = `r n1`

p-value: `r round(mod_split$p.value, 4)`

Difference in rate: `r diff_conv_rate`


## (4b) Two thousand broken experiments
```{r}
set.seed(6101)

res <- replicate(2000, {
  v <- make_users(40000)                         # engagement
  arm <- sample(rep(0:1, each = nrow(v) / 2))    # arm
  conv <- convert(p_convert(v$engagement))       # conversion
  lost <- arm == 1 & v$engagement < -0.5 & runif(nrow(v)) < 0.30   # the loss

  keep <- !lost
  n1 <- sum(arm[keep] == 1); n0 <- sum(arm[keep] == 0)
  k1 <- sum(conv[keep & arm == 1]); k0 <- sum(conv[keep & arm == 0])

  p_split <- chisq.test(c(n0, n1), p = c(0.5, 0.5))$p.value
  pt <- prop.test(c(k1, k0), c(n1, n0), correct = FALSE)
  c(p_split = p_split, diff = k1 / n1 - k0 / n0, p_comp = pt$p.value)
})
res <- t(res)    # 2000 x 3

mean(res[, "p_split"] < 0.001)                               # share with split p < 0.001
mean(res[, "diff"] > 0 & res[, "p_comp"] < 0.05)             # treatment ahead, p < 0.05
mean(res[, "diff"])                                          # mean difference


```
All 2000 experiments gave p < 0.0001. The treatment lead in `r mean(res[, "diff"] > 0 & res[, "p_comp"] < 0.05) `, with a mean difference of `r mean(res[, "diff"]) `.



## (4c) Rebalancing, and what to do instead
```{r}
# Single experiment from a
set.seed(6101)
v <- make_users(40000)
v$arm <- sample(rep(0:1, each = nrow(v) / 2))
v$converted <- convert(p_convert(v$engagement))
lost <- v$arm == 1 & v$engagement < -0.5 & runif(nrow(v)) < 0.30
logged <- v[!lost, ]

# Rebalance: drop control users at random until the arms are equal
n_treat <- sum(logged$arm == 1)
ctrl_rows <- which(logged$arm == 0)
set.seed(6101)                                   # immediately before the sample()
keep_ctrl <- sample(ctrl_rows, n_treat)          # keep n_treat control users
bal <- logged[c(keep_ctrl, which(logged$arm == 1)), ]

table(bal$arm)                                   # should now be equal
k1 <- sum(bal$converted[bal$arm == 1]); n1 <- sum(bal$arm == 1)
k0 <- sum(bal$converted[bal$arm == 0]); n0 <- sum(bal$arm == 0)
k1 / n1 
k0 / n0
k1 / n1 - k0 / n0
prop.test(c(k1, k0), c(n1, n0), correct = FALSE)
```


In A, the comparison was not based on users randomized, then the loss removed low-engagement users from the treatment only so the arms differed before the added feature is actually implemented. For 2000 replicates, the mean difference was `r mean(res[, "diff"]) ` percentage points and treatment came out ahead in `r mean(res[, "diff"] > 0 & res[, "p_comp"] < 0.05) * 100`% experiments. Even after dropping control users, the difference was `r k1 / n1 - k0 / n0` percentage points with the treatment arm missing low-engagement users, so rebalancing did nothing. Stopping after seeing a split test and not reporting the conversion comparison would be my recommendation, and then make sure the assignment is recorded and rerun the experiment.



# Part 5 · Randomize users, count sessions (16 points)

```{r}
z    <- rnorm(2000)
arm  <- rep(0:1, each = 1000)
k    <- 1 + rpois(2000, 5)          # sessions per user
pu   <- plogis(-2 + z)              # each user's own chance per session
conv <- rbinom(2000, k, pu)         # converting sessions per user
```


## (5a) Sessions as the unit
```{r}
set.seed(6101)

p_sess <- replicate(2000, {
  z    <- rnorm(2000)
  arm  <- rep(0:1, each = 1000)
  k    <- 1 + rpois(2000, 5)
  pu   <- plogis(-2 + z)
  conv <- rbinom(2000, k, pu)

  k1 <- sum(conv[arm == 1]); n1 <- sum(k[arm == 1])   # converting sessions / sessions, treatment
  k0 <- sum(conv[arm == 0]); n0 <- sum(k[arm == 0])   # control
  prop.test(c(k1, k0), c(n1, n0), correct = FALSE)$p.value
})

mean(p_sess < 0.05)    # false-positive rate
```
False positive rate: `r mean(p_sess < 0.05) `
Sessions from the same user are correlated, but assumed to be independent, thus the large false-positive rate.

## (5b) Users as the unit
```{r}
set.seed(6101)

p_both <- replicate(2000, {
  z    <- rnorm(2000)
  arm  <- rep(0:1, each = 1000)
  k    <- 1 + rpois(2000, 5)
  pu   <- plogis(-2 + z)
  conv <- rbinom(2000, k, pu)

  # (a) session level
  k1 <- sum(conv[arm == 1]); n1 <- sum(k[arm == 1])
  k0 <- sum(conv[arm == 0]); n0 <- sum(k[arm == 0])
  p_a <- prop.test(c(k1, k0), c(n1, n0), correct = FALSE)$p.value

  # (b) user level: each user's conversion rate
  rate <- conv / k
  p_b <- t.test(rate[arm == 1], rate[arm == 0])$p.value

  c(p_a, p_b)
})

mean(p_both[1, ] < 0.05)   # (a) should reproduce 0.1255
mean(p_both[2, ] < 0.05)   # (b) user-level false-positive rate
```
False-positive rate: `r mean(p_both[2, ] < 0.05) `
Randomizing users brought the false positive rate down to the desired 0.05 level as intended by design.


## (5c) Which step failed

Step 2 failed as the observations were not independent, but correlated. When randomizing the correct unit, the user, making the observations independent. It brought the false positive rate down to be aligned with the assumption of independence and the 0.05 rate (`r mean(p_both[2, ] < 0.05) `). Previously, the draw was not a random sample of flights but of days (16 flights per day), which violates independence. The same solution applies here with appropriately randomizing the unit of interest, the user.


# Part 6 · The report (12 points)
```{r}
set.seed(6101)

n <- ceiling(pw_05$n)      # 37,426 per arm

z    <- rnorm(2 * n)
arm  <- rep(0:1, each = n)
conv <- convert(p_convert(z, treated = arm, lift = 0.003))
```

## (6a) One experiment
```{r}
k1 <- sum(conv[arm == 1]); n1 <- sum(arm == 1)
k0 <- sum(conv[arm == 0]); n0 <- sum(arm == 0)

k1 / n1                    # treatment rate
k0 / n0                    # control rate
k1 / n1 - k0 / n0          # difference, treatment minus control

pt <- prop.test(c(k1, k0), c(n1, n0), correct = FALSE)
pt$conf.int                # 95% interval for the difference
pt$p.value
```

Treatment rate: `r round(k1 / n1, 3) `

Control rate: `r round(k0 / n0, 3)`

Difference: `r round(k1 / n1 - k0 / n0, 3) `

95% interval: `r round(pt$conf.int, 3)`

p-value: `r round(pt$p.value, 3)`

## (6b) The sentence, and two that are wrong
```{r}
rate1  <- k1 / n1                          # treatment rate
rate0  <- k0 / n0                          # control rate
diff   <- rate1 - rate0                    # treatment minus control
ci     <- pt$conf.int                      # interval for the difference
pval   <- pt$p.value
thresh <- 0.005                            # product manager's threshold

pp <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(x * 100, format = "f", digits = d)   # proportion -> percentage points
fmt_p <- function(p) if (p < 0.001) "< 0.001" else formatC(p, format = "f", digits = 2)

# power of this design for the true 0.3-point lift
pw_lift <- power.prop.test(n = n, p1 = p0, p2 = p0 + 0.003, sig.level = 0.05)$power
```


In a test involving `r format(n, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)` users in each group, the feature increased the estimated conversion rate by `r pp(diff)` percentage points (`r pp(rate1)`% compared with `r pp(rate0)`%). However, the 95% confidence interval ranges from `r pp(ci[1])` to +`r pp(ci[2])` percentage points (p ≈ `r fmt_p(pval)`). This means the results are compatible with both no effect and a positive effect exceeding the `r pp(thresh, 1)`-percentage-point threshold. Therefore, the test does not provide enough evidence to determine whether the feature meets the desired threshold.

1. "The feature has no effect because the result was not statistically significant (p = 0.19)."
This conclusion is incorrect. A p-value greater than 0.05 does not demonstrate that the feature has no effect; it simply means the results do not provide sufficient evidence to rule out zero effect. Furthermore, the confidence interval extends to +0.58 percentage points, meaning an improvement greater than the 0.5-point threshold remains plausible.

2. "There is a 95% probability that the true effect is between -0.12 and +0.58 percentage points."
This interpretation is also incorrect. The true effect is a fixed value, not a probability distribution. The 95% confidence level refers to the long-run reliability of the method: if we repeated the experiment many times, approximately 95% of the confidence intervals constructed using this method would contain the true effect.
